texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Abstract
texts.text: Abstract

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The M protein of group A streptococci (Strep A) is a major virulence determinant and protective antigen. The N-terminal region of the M protein is variable in sequence, defines the M/emm type, and contains epitopes that elicit opsonic antibodies that protect animals from challenge infections. Although there are >200 M types of Strep A, there is now evidence that structurally related M proteins can be grouped into clusters and that immunity may be cluster-specific in addition to M type-specific. This observation has led to recent studies of structure-based design of multivalent M peptide vaccines to select peptides predicted to cross-react with heterologous M types to improve vaccine coverage. In the current study, we have applied a refined series of peptide structural algorithms to predict immunological cross-reactivity among 117 N-terminal M peptides representing the most prevalent M types of Strep A. Based on the results of the structural analyses, in combination with global M type prevalence data, we constructed a 32-valent vaccine containing 19 cross-reactive vaccine candidates predicted to cross-react with 37 heterologous M peptides to which were added 13 type-specific M peptides. The 4-protein recombinant vaccine was immunogenic in rabbits and elicited significant levels of antibodies against 31/32 (97%) vaccine

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 1. Introduction
texts.text: 1. Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Group A streptococcus (Strep A) is a human-specific pathogen that is responsible for a significant disease burden worldwide [1]. Efforts to develop vaccines to prevent Strep A infections and their complications have been ongoing for many decades [2]. Many have focused on the M protein as a vaccine antigen, which is a major virulence determinant and protective antigen [3]. The variable sequence N-terminal region of M protein defines the M type of Strep A and contains epitopes that elicit antibodies with the greatest opsonic activity [4] that protect animals from challenge infections [5]. We have previously constructed recombinant multivalent M protein-based vaccines containing limited N-terminal M peptides linked in tandem representing as many as 30 different M types of Strep A [6 , 7]. Clinical studies in adult volunteers have indicated that the vaccines are safe and immunogenic and elicited functional opsonic antibodies against the M types represented in the vaccines [8 , 9].
texts.text: Group A streptococcus (Strep A) is a human-specific pathogen that is responsible for a significant disease burden worldwide [1]. Efforts to develop vaccines to prevent Strep A infections and their complications have been ongoing for many decades [2]. Many have focused on the M protein as a vaccine antigen, which is a major virulence determinant and protective antigen [3]. The variable sequence N-terminal region of M protein defines the M type of Strep A and contains epitopes that elicit antibodies with the greatest opsonic activity [4] that protect animals from challenge infections [5]. We have previously constructed recombinant multivalent M protein-based vaccines containing limited N-terminal M peptides linked in tandem representing as many as 30 different M types of Strep A [6 , 7]. Clinical studies in adult volunteers have indicated that the vaccines are safe and immunogenic and elicited functional opsonic antibodies against the M types represented in the vaccines [8 , 9].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One challenge in developing multivalent M peptide vaccines is the number of M/emm types (>200), each of which by definition expresses a surface M protein with a different N-terminal peptide sequence. Given the diversity of the epidemiology of Strep A infections, especially in populations at high risk for rheumatic heart disease (RHD) [10 , 11], even complex multivalent vaccines may not achieve satisfactory levels of M type coverage. It has been widely held for many years that immunity to Strep A is type-specific and infection with one M type confers protection only against the infecting type. However, with the advent of emm sequencing, it has become evident that the majority of M types are structurally related and can be grouped into sequence-based clusters that share host protein binding characteristics [12]. This observation and our previous results showing that a 30-valent vaccine elicited antibodies that cross-opsonized multiple "non-vaccine" M types [6] prompted us to take a structure-based approach to the design of multivalent M peptide vaccines [13–15].

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Our approach is based on the concept that Immunity to GAS infections is a combination of "cluster-specific" and "type-specific" immune responses that depend on the sequence-related conformational properties of the M epitopes concerned. Our hypothesis is that broadly protective vaccines can be developed using structure-guided design that takes full advantage of the structural relatedness of M peptides. The overall goal of the current study was to develop and validate a set of structural algorithms that would predict which M peptides are Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript most likely to elicit cross-opsonic antibodies against non-vaccine M types, thus increasing the potential emm type coverage of the vaccine.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2.1 Peptide structure-based algorithms used for vaccine design
texts.text: 2.1 Peptide structure-based algorithms used for vaccine design

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Antibodies bind to epitopes in three dimensions. Our hypothesis is that 3D structure is more predictive of antibody binding than sequence alone. Therefore, similarity in epitope 3D structure between two sequence-related M peptides is hypothesized to predict antibody cross-reactivity. Here, we used a set of structural criteria shown to predict with high specificity the likelihood of eliciting significant levels of cross-reactive antibodies between pairs of sequence-related heterologous M peptides [13–15]. Previous studies have identified 117 sequence-related N-terminal M peptides from M types that are responsible for >90% of Strep A infections globally [14]. After assessing pairwise sequence identity of all 117 peptides, additional criteria considered the empirical heptad identity scores of the peptide pairs, the length of the predicted coiled-coil region and the degree of coiled-coil propensity. The empirical heptad score acts as a descriptor that captures the degree of sequence and structural similarity between a pair of coiled-coil peptides. The score makes use of the fact that coiled-coil structures are adopted by the majority of M-protein sequences which have structural repeats every seven residues. To determine the heptad score between peptide pairs, we established the heptad register with MARCOIL [16] and then calculated the pairwise heptad score as the sum of the weights associated with the sequence identity at each of the polar heptad positions as calculated by the Needleman Wunsch algorithm [17]. The hydrophobic core residues were not included as they were assumed to be less accessible for antibody binding. Each possible cross-reactive peptide-pair was further classified into four classes based on the length of the shortest predicted coiled-coil region of the peptide in the pair and the lowest coiled-coil propensity of the peptide in the pair. Peptides in Class 1 pairs had long coiled-coil regions (>35aa) and the lowest coiled-coil propensity of either peptide in the pair was 20%−50%, Class 2 pairs had peptides that each had long coiled-coil regions (>35aa) and high coiled-coil propensity (>50%). Peptide pairs in Class 3 had a minimum length of coiled-coil regions of 25–34 aa and moderate to high coiled-coil propensity (>25%). Class 4 pairs contained at least one peptide with a short coiled-coil region (<25 aa) and/or low coiled-coil probability (<20%). Class 4 pairs were not predicted to cross-react. Class 1 and Class 2 pairs were predicted to cross-react if the coiled-coil region sequence identity was >50% and the empirical heptad score was >10. Class 3 pairs were predicted to cross-react if the coiled-coil region sequence identity was >55% and the empirical heptad score was >13.5.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Three female New Zealand white rabbits (Charles River, Wilmington, MA, USA) were immunized intramuscularly with 400 μg of the vaccine (100 μg of each protein) mixed with squalene-in-water (Addavax, InvivoGen, San Diego, CA, USA) containing 25 μg of monophosphorylated lipid A (MPL, InvivoGen) at time 0, 4, and 8 weeks. A booster injection was given at 18 weeks and serum was obtained 2, 3, and 4 weeks after the final injection and pooled. The pooled immune serum from individual rabbits was used in all of the following antibody assays.

texts.text: 2.5 HL-60 opsonophagocytic killing (OPK) assays

texts.label: text
texts.orig: OPK assays were performed in quadruplicate using HL-60 cells as effector phagocytes and baby rabbit serum as a source of complement, as previously described [20]. Percent killing was calculated using the formula: [(total CFU with normal rabbit serum (NRS))-(CFU with immune serum)/(total CFU with NRS) × 100]. Data were reported as the average percent killing in quadruplicate assays +/− the standard deviation calculated after averaging the CFU in the four control samples.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 3.1 Vaccine design
texts.text: 3.1 Vaccine design

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Applying the sequence and structure-based criteria for predicting peptide cross-reactivity to the hypervariable N-terminal 1–50 residues of 117 M proteins, we identified 69 crossreactive M peptide pairs and 72 emm types that were predicted to cross-react with one or more emm types (Supplemental Data, Table 1). We initially selected the minimum number of M peptides that based on cross-reactivity would theoretically cover all 72 emm types which resulted in a 25-valent hypothetical vaccine that would cover the remaining 48 crossreactive non-vaccine emm types. However, the predicted global coverage for these 73 emm types as calculated using the regional epidemiological data [17] was low and uneven across the different geographic regions. Therefore, we retained the top 19 cross-reactive vaccine candidates from the 72 cross-reactive emm types and added 13 type-specific M peptides based on their prevalence (Fig. 1 and Supplemental Data, Table 2). The 19 selected emm types were predicted to cross react with 37 heterologous emm types and, in combination with the 13 type-specific M peptides, provide theoretical M-type coverage of 90% globally.

texts.orig: 3.2 Immunogenicity of the 32-valent vaccine
texts.text: 3.2 Immunogenicity of the 32-valent vaccine

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Three rabbits were immunized with the 32-valent vaccine formulated in squalene-in-water plus MPL. The vaccine was highly immunogenic and elicited significant levels of antibodies against the N-terminal synthetic peptides contained in the vaccine (Fig. 2). Maximum serum antibody titers in any of the three immunized rabbits ranged from 400 to 102,400. Antibody levels in at least one of three antisera increased by 8-fold or greater over pre-immune levels against 31 of 32 (97%) vaccine peptides. Of the 96 titers determined (3 rabbit antisera × 32 peptides), 80 (83%) demonstrated at least an 8-fold increase in antibody levels.

texts.orig: 3.3 Cross-reactive M peptide antibodies elicited by the vaccine
texts.text: 3.3 Cross-reactive M peptide antibodies elicited by the vaccine

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The M peptides included in the 32-valent vaccine were predicted to cross-react with Nterminal M peptides of 37 non-vaccine emm types of Strep A (Fig. 1). At least 1 of the 3 immune rabbit sera contained significant levels of antibodies (≥8-fold) against 28/37 (76%) non-vaccine M peptides (Fig. 3). Antibody levels in one or more of the three antisera increased by 4-fold over pre-immune levels against 34/37 (92%) non-vaccine peptides. To assess the accuracy of the structural algorithms used to select the cross-reactive peptide pairs, the immune sera were also assayed for cross-reactivity against the remaining 48/117 M peptides not predicted to share epitopes with the vaccine peptides. Antibody titers of ≥400 were observed with 3/48 peptides (M13, M15, and M96) (data not shown).
texts.text: The M peptides included in the 32-valent vaccine were predicted to cross-react with Nterminal M peptides of 37 non-vaccine emm types of Strep A (Fig. 1). At least 1 of the 3 immune rabbit sera contained significant levels of antibodies (≥8-fold) against 28/37 (76%) non-vaccine M peptides (Fig. 3). Antibody levels in one or more of the three antisera increased by 4-fold over pre-immune levels against 34/37 (92%) non-vaccine peptides. To assess the accuracy of the structural algorithms used to select the cross-reactive peptide pairs, the immune sera were also assayed for cross-reactivity against the remaining 48/117 M peptides not predicted to share epitopes with the vaccine peptides. Antibody titers of ≥400 were observed with 3/48 peptides (M13, M15, and M96) (data not shown).

texts.orig: To determine the potential coverage of the 32-valent vaccine, we combined the predicted or observed M peptide cross-reactive immune responses to the 32-valent vaccine together with the recent compilation of Strep A emm type prevalence in regions of the world [19]. The potential global coverage based on the M types included in the vaccine and predicted cross-reactive antibody responses was estimated to be 90% (Table 1). However, regional Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript coverage ranged from 68% in Africa and Oceania to 95% in North America. Applying observed antibody responses (≥8-fold) resulted in 86% predicted emm type coverage in the world, with a range of 60% in Africa to 91% in Asia and the Pacific.

texts.orig: Opsonophagocytic killing assays were performed to assess the functional activity of the 32-valent vaccine immune responses (Fig. 4). Twenty-nine of the 32 vaccine emm types and 29/37 emm types predicted to cross-react with the 32-valent vaccine antisera were assessed in HL-60 killing assays. Only emm types that met the pre-established criteria for growth in the control mixtures (≥4 generations) were included in the analysis. Assays with each M type were performed in quadruplicate with each of the three rabbit antisera and only the antiserum resulting in the highest mean killing value is reported. Killing of ≥30% was observed for 21/29 vaccine emm types tested (Fig. 4). Some level of killing (≥10%) was achieved with 28/29 vaccine emm types. The mean level of killing for all vaccine emm types tested was 46% (range 0–98%). Of the 29 cross-reactive emm types tested, 12 resulted in killing ≥30% and the mean killing was 29% (range 0–81%).

texts.orig: 4. Discussion
texts.text: 4. Discussion

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The search for safe, effective and affordable vaccines to prevent Strep A infections and their complications has been ongoing for decades. Obstacles to vaccine development include the complex biology of Strep A, the variability of the host response to infection, the possibility of autoimmunity triggered by vaccines, and the lack of a defined human immune correlate of protection. Currently there are two general approaches to vaccine formulation. One involves the identification of protective antigens that are shared by most or all M types of Strep A and the other is formulating multiple N-terminal M peptides in multivalent vaccines targeting the most prevalent emm types [2]. While M antibodies protect against infection in several animal models [5], the challenge has been to develop multivalent vaccines that would provide optimal coverage against the >200 emm types of Strep A.

texts.orig: In recent studies, we have taken a structure-based approach to capitalize on the immunological relatedness of M proteins [13–15]. The observation that the majority of M proteins are structurally related to others has led to the concept of M clusters [12]. Within a cluster, the sequence-related M proteins also share host protein binding characteristics. It is likely that the requirement to bind specific host proteins, which is associated with the virulence of different M types within a cluster, serves to constrain the structures which contributes to immunological cross-reactivity. We have previously tested this hypothesis by applying structure-based analyses to three different clusters of M proteins in an effort to minimize the total number of vaccine M peptides necessary to elicit functional immune responses (opsonophagocytic killing) against the non-vaccine emm types of Strep A in the cluster. The process is iterative and requires postulating structural determinants likely to predict cross-reactive antibody binding between pairs of M peptides, formulating vaccines containing the minimum number of peptides predicted to cross-react with all emm types in the cluster, testing the vaccines to empirically determine the cross-reactivity among the M

texts.orig: In the current study, we have further refined the suite of analytical tools used to predict which M peptides are most likely to elicit antibodies that cross-react with heterologous non-vaccine emm types of Strep A. Rather than starting with pre-defined clusters of M peptides, we applied the new set of structural analyses to 117 N-terminal M peptides from emm types of Strep A that are most prevalent in the world [14]. We used the criteria of sequence identity, coiled-coil length and propensity, plus heptad identity scores to predict the likelihood that two peptides would display immunological cross reactivity. For practical reasons related to the size of recombinant vaccine proteins, the number of potential crossreactive peptides in the vaccine was down-selected based on the global and geographic prevalence of M types [17]. The addition of type-specific peptides to increase the potential coverage of the vaccine was likewise based on M type prevalence.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The 32-valent vaccine elicited antibodies that cross-reacted with 28/37 peptides (76%) predicted by the structural algorithms. When the antisera were assayed against the 48 M peptides that were not predicted to share epitopes, cross-reactions were observed against 3/48 (6%) of the remaining peptides. These results indicate favorable positive and negative predictive values of the structural criteria used to select the vaccine peptides. Improving the predictive power of the analyses will require additional iterations of the process using even more precise structural criteria. Co-crystallization studies with cross-reactive antibodies and peptides may shed light on new structural features involved in cross-reactive epitope conformations.

texts.orig: In this study, we used an HL-60 cell OPK assay to determine the functional activity of antibodies elicited by the 32-valent vaccine. We have previously shown that results of the HL-60 assay are generally comparable to those achieved with the classical Lancefield whole human blood assay [20]. However, the HL-60 assay also appears to be a less sensitive, yet more specific indicator of functional antibody activity compared to the whole blood assay because of the presence of naturally acquired Strep A antibodies in human blood. There is not an established correlation between the absolute level of bacterial killing promoted by immune sera and protection against infection. The establishment of an immune correlate will require advanced clinical trials designed to assess the efficacy of vaccines in preventing Strep A infections and simultaneous determinations of OPK activity, and potentially additional immune signatures such as T-cell responses and cytokine profiles. Nonetheless, in the current study we observed functional antibody activity against the majority of vaccine and non-vaccine M types tested.

texts.orig: The predicted global M type coverage of the 32-valent vaccine was estimated using a data set of M type prevalence of Strep A recently curated from the literature [17]. The results for some geographic regions and those of global coverage are likely skewed by the relative paucity of molecular epidemiologic studies in low- and middle-income regions of the world. Of the 77,068 emm types of Strep A included in the analysis, the vast majority were reported from North America (47%), Europe (29%), Asia-Pacific (12%), and Oceania (9%). The lower levels of coverage predicted in Africa, Arab countries, South Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript America, and Oceania are well below the 90% efficacy target stated in the Strep A Preferred Product Characteristics recently outlined by the WHO [21]. Nonetheless, coverage of even 60% of infections may eventually translate into a significant impact on the morbidity and mortality associated with Strep A infections and their complications. Continued efforts to identify structural algorithms that predict which M peptides are likely to cross-react with heterologous M types of Strep A should further enhance the potential coverage and efficacy of M protein-based vaccines, especially in regions of the world with populations at high risk for ARF and RHD.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: 32-valent vaccine designed to elicit broadly cross-reactive antibodies against heterologous M peptides. The vaccine contained 19 M peptides predicted to elicit cross-reactive immunity to an additional 37 M types (listed under the respective vaccine peptide), plus 13 M peptides from prevalent M types that were not predicted to cross-react with others but were included to increase potential vaccine coverage. M67 and M11 were each predicted to elicit crossreactive antibodies against M44, M65, and M85 peptides. M2, M5, and M6 peptides were 25 aa in length and repeated in tandem (x2) for a total length of 50 aa.
